steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on using forwards-backwards dynamics models to approximate MDP homomorphisms in reinforcement learning. It should motivate the sample efficiency problem, explain the idea of equivalent effect abstraction, list our contributions, and discuss how it relates to prior work.

However, RL is computationally expensive and this hinders deploying it in the real world. RL can need hundreds of millions of samples to learn a policy, either within an environment model or by interacting directly. Sample efficiency is improving, but there is still a gap between the agents that perform best and the ones that are sample efficient.

Humans abstract away the details about state-action pairs that do not effect their values. Previous works hard code homomorphisms into a policy, but approaches that learn homomorphic mappings online from experience are an active area of research.

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Reinforcement learning (RL) has reached superhuman performance on benchmarks that were previously unsolvable, such as Go and Starcraft. However, RL is computationally expensive and this hinders deploying it in the real world. RL can need hundreds of millions of samples to learn a policy, either within an environment model or by interacting directly. Sample efficiency is improving, but there is still a gap between the agents that perform best and the ones that are sample efficient.

Humans abstract away the details about state-action pairs that do not effect their values. For example, in the Atari game Asterix an agent collects gold while avoiding enemies in a 2D navigation task. A human gamer understands that collecting treasure when coming from below has the same value as collecting the same treasure when coming from the right (figure 1), and this lets them progress more quickly because they generalise value predictions between equivalent state-action pairs. In this work we identify this abstraction as a Markov decision process (MDP) homomorphism. MDP homomorphisms collapse the equivalent state-actions in an observed MDP onto a smaller abstract state-action space in an abstract MDP.

If we have a mapping to an abstract MDP, policies can be learned efficiently in the smaller abstract space and then mapped back to the experienced MDP when interacting with the environment. Previous works hard code homomorphisms into a policy, but approaches that learn homomorphic mappings online from experience are an active area of research.

We present equivalent effect abstraction, which is a method for constructing MDP homomorphisms from experience using a partial dynamics model of state transitions (without having to predict rewards). It uses the fact that state-action pairs which lead to the same next state frequently have equivalent values. We use this insight in off-policy value-based RL, which is the most sample efficient class of RL algorithms for discrete control. Off-policy RL predicts separate values for the different actions in a given state. We make it more sample efficient by only requiring the value function to predict the value of a single action that the practitioner selects, which we call the hypothetical action, in a separate state that we call a hypothetical state. To compute the hypothetical state, we first move through a forwards dynamics model with a given state-action pair. Then we move backwards through a model that predicts which hypothetical state would lead to the same next state as the original state-action pair, if the hypothetical action was selected.

Going back to the Asterix example, moving to a given state has the same value whether the previous action was right, left, up or down. So, if we have a dynamics model, we show that if the value of approaching a state from the right is known, the value of approaching the same state from the left, below, or above can also be deduced. This means equivalent effect abstraction extrapolates value judgements between equivalent state-action pairs, which reduces how much experience is needed to learn a policy. Our contributions are the following.

- 1. We develop a new approach for learning a reduced MDP without knowing the symmetries, and we prove that, under certain assumptions, our mapping to the reduced MDP is a homomorphism.

- 2. We confirm these theoretical results in an idealised tabular setting, where we show that equivalent effect abstraction improves the planning efficiency of model-based RL and also the sample efficiency of model-free RL.

- 3. In the deep RL setting, we test our approach when the homomorphism is only approximate because of imperfect learned models. We show an improvement over standard baselines on the Cartpole and Predator-Prey environments (which are MDP homomorphisms benchmarks from earlier work).

- 4. In the MinAtar suite, where the assumptions needed for our theoretical results are violated even more (especially the ones about stochasticity), we find an almost 4x improvement over a value based baseline at 250k frames (when all results are averaged over different optimizers and games).

We are not the first ones to exploit the equivalence of state action pairs that lead to the same next state. A backgammon program uses the concept of afterstates (states immediately before an opponents response to an action). This is similar to our approach, and it has been scaled within MuZero to other board games, but in general afterstates have not found wider applicability. Kinematic inseparability is a related but distinct abstraction which uses contrastive learning to classify whether two states will lead to the same next state for the same action. Our approach instead looks for state-action pairs (with different actions) that lead to the same next state, and this is a broader form of abstraction. Another difference is that equivalent effect abstraction does not need the states to be discrete, so it can readily be applied to common RL environments where it is rare to reach the same state twice. Finally, one more work defines a state-action equivalence that is more comprehensive than the equivalence defined in prior homomorphism work. It is satisfied by various equivalent state-action pairs like the ones found in earlier works and also by the state-action pairs satisfying the equivalent effect abstraction we present. However, they assume that a tree of discrete states can be searched over for equivalences, and this is challenging in deep RL.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved superhuman performance on previously unsolvable benchmarks such as Go [1] and Starcraft [2]. However, the computational expense of RL hinders its deployment in the real world. RL can require hundreds of millions of samples to learn a policy, either within an environment model [3] or through direct interaction [4]. While sample efficiency is improving, there is still a gap between the best performing agents and those that are sample efficient [5,6].

Humans abstract away details about state-action pairs that do not effect their values. Consider the Atari game Asterix, where an agent collects gold while avoiding enemies in a 2D navigation task. A human gamer understands that collecting treasure when approaching from below has the same value as collecting the same treasure when approaching from the right (figure 1), which lets them progress more quickly by generalising value predictions between equivalent state-action pairs. In this work, we identify this abstraction as a Markov decision process (MDP) homomorphism [8,9]. MDP homomorphisms collapse equivalent state-actions in an observed MDP onto a smaller abstract state-action space in an abstract MDP [9].

Given a mapping to an abstract MDP, policies can be learned efficiently in the smaller abstract space and then mapped back to the experienced MDP when interacting with the environment [8]. Previous works hard code homomorphisms into a policy [9], but developing approaches that learn homomorphic mappings online from experience is an active area of research [10,11].

We present equivalent effect abstraction, a method for constructing MDP homomorphisms from experience via a partial dynamics model of state transitions (without needing to predict rewards), leveraging the fact that state-action pairs leading to the same next state frequently have equivalent values. We use this insight in off-policy value-based RL, the most sample efficient class of RL algorithms for discrete control [5]. Off-policy RL predicts separate values for different actions in a given state. We further improve sample efficiency by only requiring a value function to predict the value of a single action selected by the practitioner, which we call the hypothetical action, in a separate state called a hypothetical state. The hypothetical state is computed by first moving through a forwards dynamics model with a given state-action pair, and then moving backwards through a model that predicts what hypothetical state would lead to the same next state as the original state-action pair, given that the hypothetical action was selected.

Consider again the Asterix example: moving to a given state has the same value whether your previous action was right, left, up or down. Thus, equipped with a dynamics model, we show that if the value of approaching a state from the right is known, the value of approaching the same state from the left, below, or above can also be deduced. Equivalent effect abstraction therefore extrapolates value judgements between equivalent state-action pairs, reducing the amount of experience required to learn a policy. We make the following contributions.

- 1. We develop a novel approach for learning a reduced MDP without knowledge of symmetries, and prove that, under certain assumptions, our mapping to the reduced MDP is a homomorphism.

- 2. We confirm these theoretical results in an idealised tabular setting, showing that equivalent effect abstraction improves the planning efficiency of model-based RL and the sample efficiency of model-free RL.

- 3. In the deep RL setting, we test our approach when the homomorphism is approximate due to imperfect learned models, and show an improvement over standard baselines on Cartpole and Predator-Prey environments (MDP homomorphisms benchmarks from [9]).

- 4. In the MinAtar suite [12], where the assumptions required for our theoretical results are further violated (especially those relating to stochasticity), we find an almost 4x improvement over a value based baseline at 250k frames (averaging all results over different optimizers and games).

We are not the first to exploit the equivalence of state action pairs that lead to the same next state. [13] use the concept of afterstates (states immediately before an opponents response to an action [14]) in their backgammon program. This is similar to our approach and has been scaled within MuZero to other board games [14], but afterstates have generally not found wider applicability. [15] ’s kinematic inseparability is a related but distinct abstraction that uses contrastive learning to classify whether two states will lead to the same next state for the same action. Our approach, in contrast, looks for state-action pairs (with different actions) that lead to the same next state, which is a broader form of abstraction. Another difference is that equivalent effect abstraction does not require states to be discrete, making it readily applicable to common RL environments where it is rare to reach the same state twice. Finally, [16] defines a state-action equivalence that is more comprehensive than the equivalence defined by [8], and which is satisfied by various equivalent state-action pairs like those found in [8,9,15] as well as by the state-action pairs satisfying our equivalent effect abstraction. However, they assume that a tree of discrete states can be searched over for equivalences, which is challenging in deep RL.
